subject: ielts
title: True / False / Not Given
summary: Как отличать «противоречит тексту» от «не сказано» — главный источник потерь баллов в Reading.
theory:
## Три ответа и их смысл
**TRUE** — утверждение полностью совпадает с информацией в тексте (пусть и другими словами).
**FALSE** — текст говорит **противоположное**: есть прямое противоречие.
**NOT GIVEN** — в тексте об этом просто нет информации: ни подтверждения, ни опровержения.

Главная ошибка русскоязычных: ставить FALSE там, где нужно NOT GIVEN. Спрашивай себя: «Могу ли я показать пальцем предложение, которое это опровергает?» Если не можешь — это NOT GIVEN.

## Алгоритм
1. Читай утверждения **по порядку** — они идут в порядке текста.
2. Найди ключевое слово (имя, число, термин) в тексте.
3. Сравни утверждение и предложение текста **по частям**: подлежащее, действие, количество, время.
4. Ищи слова-модификаторы: *all, only, always, never, the first, the most* — они часто и делают утверждение ложным.

:::warn Ловушки
- **«Some» против «all»**: текст говорит *some researchers*, утверждение — *all researchers* → FALSE.
- **Сравнение, которого нет**: текст описывает два явления, утверждение говорит, что одно *важнее* другого. Если сравнения в тексте нет → NOT GIVEN.
- **Причина, которой нет**: текст называет два факта, утверждение связывает их словом *because*. Если связи в тексте нет → NOT GIVEN.
- **Мнение вместо факта**: *scientists believe* ≠ *it is proven*.
:::

:::tip Правила игры
- Отвечать нужно ровно словами TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN (или YES / NO / NOT GIVEN для YNNG-вопросов).
- Нельзя оставлять пропуски: если не знаешь — ставь NOT GIVEN, это самый частый ответ среди «сомнительных».
- Не используй свои знания о мире. Только текст.
- На все 13–14 вопросов passage даётся около 20 минут.
:::

## Разница TFNG и YNNG
TFNG проверяет **факты**, YNNG — **взгляды автора** (в текстах с аргументацией). Алгоритм тот же, но для YNNG ищи слова мнения: *argues, claims, in my view, undoubtedly*.
passage:
**A** For most of human history, cities grew in a single direction: outwards. As populations increased, farmland at the edge of a settlement was gradually converted into housing, and the distance between the centre and the newest districts became greater. This pattern, which planners call urban sprawl, was accelerated in the twentieth century by the private car. When people could travel fifteen kilometres to work in half an hour, there seemed little reason to live close to the office.

**B** The costs of that expansion, however, took decades to become visible. Low-density suburbs are expensive to serve: every kilometre of new road, water pipe and electricity cable must be built and then maintained, while the number of households paying for it remains small. A study of thirty North American municipalities found that the cost of providing basic services to a household in a low-density suburb was roughly two and a half times the cost in a dense inner district. Because these expenses are spread across an entire city budget, residents rarely notice who is paying for what.

**C** Environmental costs followed a similar pattern. Where destinations lie far apart, almost every journey requires a car, and transport becomes the largest single source of household emissions. Attempts to solve the resulting congestion by widening roads have generally failed. Traffic engineers describe the reason as induced demand: additional lanes reduce travel time for a short period, which encourages more people to drive, until congestion returns to its previous level. Several cities that doubled the capacity of their ring roads recorded the same average speeds within five years.

**D** Since the early 2000s, a number of municipalities have therefore tried the opposite approach, sometimes described as the compact city. Instead of extending the boundary, they encourage building on unused land inside it: former factories, car parks, railway yards. Housing is placed above shops and offices rather than in separate zones, so that daily needs lie within walking distance. Copenhagen, Vienna and Portland are frequently cited as examples, although each began from a different situation and used different legal tools.

**E** The best-known experiment of this kind is the fifteen-minute city, an idea developed by the researcher Carlos Moreno in Paris. It proposes that residents should be able to reach work, schools, healthcare, shops and green space within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. Paris has redistributed street space accordingly, converting traffic lanes into cycle paths and turning the areas around several hundred schools into car-free streets. Similar programmes have since been announced in Milan, Melbourne and Bogotá.

**F** Critics raise two objections. The first is economic: when a district becomes more attractive, rents rise, and the low-income residents who most depend on nearby services may be pushed out. Researchers in Barcelona measured rent increases of around eleven per cent in newly pedestrianised blocks over three years. The second objection concerns geography. In cities built around heavy industry, or in regions where extreme winter weather makes walking uncomfortable for months, the model may simply not apply.

**G** Supporters answer that the fifteen-minute city was never intended as a universal blueprint. Moreno himself has described it as a set of principles rather than a plan, and has argued that each city must adapt them to its own density, climate and history. What the approach does provide, its defenders say, is a measurable target. Instead of debating whether a neighbourhood feels liveable, planners can count how many services lie within a fifteen-minute walk and watch that number change from year to year.

**H** The evidence so far is mixed but not discouraging. Districts that have gained shops and clinics within walking distance show reduced car use and slightly higher rates of physical activity. Whether these changes are large enough to affect a city's total emissions is still uncertain, largely because the redesigned areas remain small compared with the suburbs that surround them. What is clear is that the century-long assumption that cities must keep growing outwards is no longer taken for granted.

questions.text: Urban sprawl began only in the twentieth century.
questions.explanation: Абзац A: города росли наружу «for most of human history», а автомобиль лишь **ускорил** этот процесс в XX веке. Текст прямо противоречит слову «only» → FALSE.

questions.text: Providing basic services to a household in a low-density suburb costs more than in a dense inner district.
questions.explanation: Абзац B: «roughly two and a half times the cost in a dense inner district» — прямое подтверждение → TRUE.

questions.text: Most residents of low-density suburbs are aware of how much their services cost.
questions.explanation: Абзац B: «residents rarely notice who is paying for what» — то есть большинство как раз не осознаёт. Утверждение противоречит тексту → FALSE.

questions.text: The study of thirty North American municipalities was carried out by a government agency.
questions.explanation: Абзац B упоминает исследование, но ничего не говорит о том, кто его проводил. Ни подтверждения, ни опровержения → NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Widening roads has usually failed to solve congestion in the long term.
questions.explanation: Абзац C: «Attempts to solve the resulting congestion by widening roads have generally failed», далее объясняется induced demand → TRUE.

questions.text: Cars are more harmful to the environment than heating homes in every city.
questions.explanation: Абзац C говорит, что транспорт — крупнейший источник выбросов домохозяйств там, где расстояния велики, но сравнения с отоплением и утверждения «в каждом городе» в тексте нет → NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Copenhagen, Vienna and Portland all used the same legal tools to become compact cities.
questions.explanation: Абзац D: «each began from a different situation and used different legal tools» — прямое противоречие → FALSE.

questions.text: Paris has turned the streets around some schools into car-free areas.
questions.explanation: Абзац E: «turning the areas around several hundred schools into car-free streets» → TRUE.

questions.text: Moreno believes the fifteen-minute city should be applied in the same way everywhere.
questions.explanation: Абзац G: он называет идею «a set of principles rather than a plan» и говорит, что каждый город должен адаптировать её → FALSE.

questions.text: Traffic engineers use the term ______ to explain why new lanes fill up with cars.
questions.explanation: Абзац C: «Traffic engineers describe the reason as induced demand».

questions.text: In Barcelona, rents in newly pedestrianised blocks rose by about ______ per cent over three years.
questions.explanation: Абзац F: «rent increases of around eleven per cent in newly pedestrianised blocks over three years».

questions.text: According to paragraph F, one objection to the compact city model is that
options: rising rents may force out low-income residents
walking is dangerous in large cities
it costs more than building new suburbs
questions.explanation: Абзац F: когда район становится привлекательнее, аренда растёт, и малообеспеченные жители «may be pushed out».

questions.text: What does paragraph H say about the evidence for compact city projects?
options: it is mixed, partly because the redesigned areas are still small
it proves the model reduces total emissions
it shows the model has failed
it has not been collected yet
questions.explanation: Абзац H: «The evidence so far is mixed but not discouraging», а неопределённость объясняется тем, что перестроенные районы малы по сравнению с пригородами.
